title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLIII
paragraphs:
“This figure hath high price: ’t was wrought with love
Ages ago in finest ivory;
Nought modish in it, pure and noble lines
Of generous womanhood that fits all time
That too is costly ware; majolica
Of deft design, to please a lordly eye:
The smile, you see, is perfect—wonderful
As mere Faience! a table ornament
To suit the richest mounting.”

Dorothea rarely went out without her husband. Occasionally, though, she drove alone into Middlemarch on the small shopping or charitable errands that fall to any comfortably wealthy woman living within three miles of a town. Two days after the scene in the Yew-tree Walk, she decided to use one of these opportunities to see Lydgate if she could. She wanted to learn whether her husband had felt some discouraging change in his symptoms which he was hiding from her, and whether he had insisted on hearing the full truth about his condition. Asking someone else for information about him made her feel almost guilty. But the fear of not knowing—of an ignorance that might make her harsh or unjust—overcame her scruples. She was certain he had passed through some inner crisis. The very next day he had begun rearranging his notes by a new method and given her a quite new role in carrying out his plan. Poor Dorothea needed to store up patience.
It was about four when she reached Lydgate’s house in Lowick Gate. Suddenly doubtful that he would be home, she wished she had written first. He was indeed out.
“Is Mrs. Lydgate at home?” asked Dorothea. So far as she knew, she had never seen Rosamond, but now remembered the marriage. Yes, Mrs. Lydgate was in.
“Then I’ll come in and speak to her, if she doesn’t mind. Would you ask whether she can see me—Mrs. Casaubon—for a few minutes?”

While the servant carried her message inside, Dorothea heard music through an open window: a few notes sung by a man, followed by a burst of elaborate runs on the piano. The runs stopped abruptly. Then the servant returned to say that Mrs. Lydgate would be pleased to receive Mrs. Casaubon.

When the drawing-room door opened and Dorothea came in, she created a contrast often seen in country life when the habits of different social ranks were less mixed than they are today. Those who know such things must tell us the exact name of the fabric she wore that mild autumn: a thin white wool, soft to the touch and to the eye. It always seemed freshly washed, scented with sweet hedges. It was always made into a long coat whose hanging sleeves were entirely out of fashion. Yet if she had appeared before a hushed audience as Imogen or Cato’s daughter, her clothes might have seemed perfectly appropriate. Grace and dignity lived in her limbs and neck. Around her simply parted hair and candid eyes, the large round poke bonnet then imposed on women looked no stranger than the golden plate we call a halo. No dramatic heroine could have aroused more interest than Mrs. Casaubon in the two people now watching her. To Rosamond she was one of the county divinities who did not mingle with Middlemarch mortals, and whose smallest details of dress or manner deserved study. Rosamond was also pleased that Mrs. Casaubon would have an opportunity to study _her_. What was the use of being exquisite unless the best judges saw you? Since receiving the highest compliments at Sir Godwin Lydgate’s, she felt entirely confident of the impression she would make on people of good birth. Dorothea offered her hand with her usual unaffected kindness and looked admiringly at Lydgate’s lovely bride. She was aware of a gentleman some distance away, but saw him only as a coated figure at the edge of her vision. He was too absorbed in the presence of one woman to consider the contrast between the two, though it would certainly have struck an untroubled observer. Both were tall, their eyes on the same level. But picture Rosamond’s childlike fairness and magnificent crown of braids, her pale blue dress so perfectly cut and fashionable that no dressmaker could view it unmoved. Add the large embroidered collar, whose price one hoped every spectator would appreciate, the rings carefully displaying her little hands, and the restrained awareness of herself which is the costly substitute for simplicity.

“Thank you for letting me interrupt you,” Dorothea said at once. “I’m anxious to see Mr. Lydgate before I go home, if I can. I hoped you might tell me where to find him, or perhaps let me wait if you expect him back soon.”
“He’s at the New Hospital,” Rosamond replied. “I don’t know when he’ll be back, but I can send for him.”

“Will you let me fetch him?” Will Ladislaw asked, stepping forward. He had picked up his hat before Dorothea came in. She flushed in surprise, but held out her hand with an unmistakably delighted smile.
“I didn’t realise it was you. I never expected to find you here.”
“Shall I go to the Hospital and tell Mr. Lydgate you’d like to see him?” Will asked.
“It would be quicker to send my carriage,” said Dorothea, “if you’d be so kind as to give the coachman the message.”

Will was going towards the door when a whole chain of connected memories flashed through Dorothea’s mind. Turning quickly, she said, “Thank you, but I’ll go myself. I don’t want to lose any time before returning home. I’ll drive to the Hospital and see Mr. Lydgate there. Please forgive me, Mrs. Lydgate. I’m very grateful to you.”

Some sudden thought had clearly seized her attention. She left almost unaware of her immediate surroundings, scarcely noticing that Will opened the door and offered his arm to take her to the carriage. She accepted his arm but said nothing. Will felt rather hurt and miserable, and could find nothing to say either. He helped her silently into the carriage. They said goodbye, and she drove off.

During the five-minute journey to the Hospital, thoughts entirely new to her came into her mind. Her decision to leave, and her distraction as she left, arose from a sudden feeling that deliberately allowing further contact with Will would be a kind of deception if she could not mention it to her husband. Already she was concealing her purpose in seeking Lydgate. This was all she had consciously thought, but a vague uneasiness had also driven her. Now, alone in the carriage, she heard again in her mind the man’s singing and accompanying piano, which she had barely noticed before. With some surprise, she found herself considering that Will Ladislaw was spending time with Mrs. Lydgate while her husband was out. Then she could not help remembering that he had spent time with her in similar circumstances. Why should that be improper? But Will was Mr. Casaubon’s relation, someone she had a duty to treat kindly. Still, perhaps there had been signs she ought to have understood: signs that Mr. Casaubon disliked his cousin’s visits during his own absence. “Perhaps I’ve been wrong about many things,” poor Dorothea told herself, as tears rolled down her cheeks and had to be wiped away quickly. Her unhappiness was confused. The image of Will, once so clear to her, had been mysteriously spoiled. Then the carriage stopped at the Hospital gate. Soon she was walking around the lawns with Lydgate, and her feelings returned to the urgent purpose that had brought her there.

Meanwhile, Will Ladislaw felt humiliated and knew exactly why. His opportunities to see Dorothea were rare. Now, for the first time, one of them had put him at a disadvantage. Previously the difficulty had simply been that he was not her chief concern. Now she had seen him in circumstances suggesting that she might not be his. He felt pushed farther away from her, into the circles of Middlemarch society that formed no part of her life. Yet that was not his fault. Naturally, since taking lodgings in town, he had made as many acquaintances as possible: his position required him to know everyone and everything. Lydgate was worth knowing more than anyone else nearby, and happened to have a musical wife well worth visiting. That was the entire explanation of the situation in which Diana had descended too unexpectedly upon her worshipper. It was humiliating. Will knew he would never have been in Middlemarch without Dorothea. Yet his position there now threatened to separate him from her by barriers of habitual feeling more destructive of mutual interest than the entire distance between Rome and Britain. Prejudices about rank and status were easy to defy when embodied in a tyrannical letter from Mr. Casaubon. But prejudices, like fragrant objects, exist in two forms, solid and intangible: solid as the pyramids, subtle as the twentieth echo of an echo, or the memory of hyacinths that once perfumed the dark. Will’s temperament made him acutely aware of these subtleties. A less perceptive man would not have sensed, as he did, that Dorothea had for the first time felt something improper in being entirely at ease with him, and that a chill had entered their silence as he took her to the carriage. Perhaps Casaubon, in his jealous hatred, had been insisting that Will had fallen beneath her socially. Damn Casaubon!
Will went back into the drawing room and picked up his hat. Looking annoyed, he approached Mrs. Lydgate, who was now sitting at her worktable, and said:
“Interrupting music or poetry is always fatal. May I come another day to finish what we were saying about performing ‘Lungi dal caro bene’?”

“I should be delighted with the lesson,” said Rosamond. “But surely you agree that this was a very beautiful interruption. I quite envy you knowing Mrs. Casaubon. Is she very intelligent? She looks as though she is.”
“Honestly, I’ve never considered it,” Will answered sulkily.
“Tertius gave exactly that answer when I first asked whether she was beautiful. What do you gentlemen think about when you’re with Mrs. Casaubon?”
“Her,” said Will, quite willing to provoke the charming Mrs. Lydgate. “With a perfect woman, you don’t think about separate qualities. You simply feel her presence.”
“I shall be jealous whenever Tertius visits Lowick,” Rosamond said with airy playfulness, her dimples showing. “He’ll come home and think nothing of me.”
“It doesn’t seem to have affected Lydgate that way so far. Mrs. Casaubon is too different from other women for comparisons.”
“I see you’re a devoted worshipper. I suppose you see her often.”
“No,” said Will, almost petulantly. “Worship is generally more theoretical than practical. But I’m practising it to excess at this very moment. I really must tear myself away.”
“Do come back some evening. Mr. Lydgate would enjoy hearing the music, and I can’t enjoy it quite as much without him.”

When her husband returned, Rosamond stood facing him, holding his coat collar in both hands. “Mr. Ladislaw was here singing with me when Mrs. Casaubon called,” she said. “He seemed annoyed. Do you think he disliked her finding him at our house? Surely your social position is at least as good as his, whatever his connection with the Casaubons.”
“No, no. If he really was annoyed, there must have been another reason. Ladislaw’s something of a gypsy. He doesn’t care about outward distinctions.”
“Apart from the music, he isn’t always very pleasant. Do you like him?”
“Yes, I think he’s a good fellow. A bit of a collection of odds and ends, but likeable.”
“You know, I think he worships Mrs. Casaubon.”
“Poor devil!” said Lydgate, smiling as he pinched his wife’s ears.

Rosamond was beginning to feel she knew a great deal about the world. In particular, she had discovered something she could scarcely have imagined as an unmarried girl except as a vague tragedy played out in old-fashioned clothes: even married women could make conquests and enslave men. Country girls at that time, including those educated at Mrs. Lemon’s, read little French literature more recent than Racine. Newspapers had not yet thrown their present magnificent light on life’s scandals. Still, vanity, with a woman’s whole mind and day at its disposal, can build abundantly on the smallest suggestions—especially the suggestion of limitless conquests. How delightful to take prisoners from the throne of marriage, a husband beside you as crown prince, though actually a subject himself! The captives would gaze up in perpetual hopelessness, probably losing their sleep, and if their appetites suffered too, so much the better. For the moment, however, Rosamond’s romance centred chiefly on her crown prince. His certain submission was pleasure enough. When he said, “Poor devil!” she asked with playful curiosity:
“Why do you say that?”
“Well, what can a man do once he starts worshipping one of you mermaids? He just neglects his work and piles up debts.”

“You certainly don’t neglect your work. You’re always at the Hospital, visiting poor patients, or thinking about some medical quarrel. And at home you always want to study your microscope and little bottles. Admit it—you prefer them to me.”

“Aren’t you ambitious enough to want your husband to become something more than a Middlemarch doctor?” Lydgate asked. He rested his hands on her shoulders and looked at her with affectionate seriousness. “I’ll make you learn my favourite lines from an old poet:

‘Why should our pride make such a fuss to live
And be forgotten? What good equals this:
To do what merits writing, and to write
What merits reading and delights the world?’
That’s what I want, Rosy: to do something worth writing about, and then write the account of it myself. A man has to work for that, my darling.”

“Of course I want you to make discoveries. Nobody could want more than I do for you to rise to an important position somewhere better than Middlemarch. You can’t say I’ve ever tried to stop your work. But we can’t live like hermits. You’re not dissatisfied with me, are you, Tertius?”
“No, my dear. I’m altogether too content.”
“But what did Mrs. Casaubon come to ask you?”
“Only about her husband’s health. But I think she’s going to be wonderfully generous to our New Hospital. I believe she’ll give us two hundred a year.”
